title: == vs equals()
short: == compares primitive values or object references; equals() expresses logical equality.
answer: For objects, == checks reference identity. equals() can be overridden for state equality. If equals is overridden, hashCode must follow the contract.
interview: == compares primitive values or object references; equals() expresses logical equality.

title: equals() and hashCode() contract
short: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
answer: Hash-based collections use hashCode to locate a bucket and equals to confirm the key. Unequal objects may collide.
followups: What breaks if hashCode is omitted?
interview: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

title: HashMap internal working
short: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.
answer: HashMap spreads the hash, maps it to a bucket and handles collisions. Modern Java can treeify heavily-collided buckets under suitable conditions. Resize redistributes entries.
interview: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
short: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.
answer: ArrayList is usually the better default. LinkedList has O(n) indexed access and only helps for specific operations/access patterns.
followups: Which is better for random access?
interview: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.

title: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet
short: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.
answer: Hash-based sets usually provide expected O(1) basic operations. TreeSet is generally O(log n).
interview: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.

title: How to create an immutable class
short: Prevent observable state changes after construction.
answer: Use private final fields, constructor initialization, no setters, defensive copies and final class where appropriate.
code: public final class User { private final String name; public User(String n){name=n;} }
interview: Prevent observable state changes after construction.

title: final vs finally vs finalize
short: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.
answer: final restricts reassignment/overriding/inheritance. finally normally executes after try/catch. Do not rely on finalize for cleanup.
interview: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.

title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions
short: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.
answer: Choose based on whether callers can reasonably recover and where errors are translated.
interview: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.

title: Try-with-resources
short: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.
answer: Resources close even when exceptions occur; close failures can be represented as suppressed exceptions.
interview: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.

title: Abstract class vs interface
short: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.
answer: Use abstract classes for genuine shared base behavior/state and interfaces for capabilities/contracts.
code:
interface Auditable{void audit();}
abstract class Base{Long id;}
interview: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.

title: Default and static interface methods
short: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.
answer: Default methods help evolve interfaces. Static interface methods are called through the interface name and are not instance overrides.
code: interface Loggable { default void log(){} static String level(){return "INFO";} }
interview: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.

title: Optional usage
short: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.
answer: It is particularly useful for return types. It should not automatically replace null in every field or parameter.
interview: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.

title: Functional interface
short: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.
answer: It can be targeted by lambdas/method references. Default and static methods do not count.
interview: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.

title: Lambda expression
short: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.
answer: Types are inferred from the target type. Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
interview: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.

title: Record
short: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.
answer: Records are final with final component references, but referenced objects can still be mutable.
interview: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.

title: Virtual threads
short: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.
answer: They make thread-per-task models practical at large concurrency. They do not make CPU work intrinsically faster.
interview: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.

title: synchronized
short: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.
answer: Only one thread holds a monitor at a time. Synchronization also establishes happens-before relationships.
interview: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.

title: volatile vs AtomicInteger
short: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.
answer: volatile does not make count++ atomic. AtomicInteger supports increment and compare-and-set style operations.
interview: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.

title: Deadlock and prevention
short: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.
answer: Prevent with consistent lock ordering, small lock scopes, avoiding nested locks and timed acquisition where appropriate.
interview: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.

title: Heap vs stack
short: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.
answer: Heap is shared and GC-managed. A stack holds method frames and local execution state.
interview: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.

title: Garbage collection
short: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.
answer: Collectors trade throughput, latency and memory footprint. Allocation rate and retention still matter.
interview: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.

title: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
short: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized.
answer: StringBuilder is normally preferred for iterative construction.
interview: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized.

title: Comparable vs Comparator
short: Comparable defines natural order; Comparator defines external ordering.
answer: Comparator supports multiple contextual sorting strategies.
interview: Comparable defines natural order; Comparator defines external ordering.

title: map vs flatMap
short: map is one-to-one transformation; flatMap transforms and flattens nested streams.
answer: flatMap is useful for one-to-many relationships.
interview: map is one-to-one transformation; flatMap transforms and flattens nested streams.

title: parallelStream
short: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.
answer: It can help sufficiently large CPU-bound independent work and hurt for blocking I/O/shared state/small data.
interview: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.

title: Microservice characteristics
short: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.
answer: Good boundaries consider business ownership and deployment independence. They add distributed-system complexity.
interview: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.

title: API Gateway vs Load Balancer
short: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.
answer: Gateways commonly handle auth, rate limits, routing and transformation.
interview: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.

title: Service discovery
short: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.
answer: Discovery can be client/server-side. Kubernetes commonly provides service discovery via DNS/services.
interview: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.

title: Sync vs async communication
short: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.
answer: Async improves buffering/decoupling but introduces eventual consistency and duplicate handling.
interview: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.

title: Saga pattern
short: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.
answer: Each service commits locally. Compensation is a new business action, not a distributed DB rollback.
interview: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.

title: Outbox pattern
short: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.
answer: A publisher sends outbox events later. Consumers still need idempotency.
interview: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.

title: Idempotency
short: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.
answer: Idempotency keys are useful for payments/order creation; persist key and outcome.
interview: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.

title: Retry policy
short: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.
answer: Use timeouts, exponential backoff and jitter. Avoid retrying non-idempotent operations without safeguards.
interview: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.

title: Bulkhead pattern
short: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.
answer: Separate executors, pools or concurrency limits reduce blast radius.
interview: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.

title: Eventual consistency
short: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.
answer: Define acceptable stale windows and user-visible intermediate states.
interview: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.

title: Resilience patterns
short: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.
answer: Each protects a different failure mode. Combining them requires careful limits to avoid retry storms.
interview: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.

title: Distributed tracing
short: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.
answer: Trace is end-to-end; spans represent operations. Propagation preserves correlation.
interview: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.

title: Microservice monitoring
short: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.
answer: Monitor rate, errors, latency, saturation, JVM, DB pools and broker lag.
interview: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.

title: API versioning
short: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.
answer: Additive changes and deprecation reduce consumer disruption.
interview: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.

title: Rate limiting
short: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.
answer: Token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding windows are common; distributed systems may need shared state.
interview: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.

title: Message broker
short: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.
answer: Kafka, RabbitMQ and cloud messaging have different ordering/delivery models.
interview: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.

title: Kafka topic/partition/group
short: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.
answer: More consumers than partitions do not increase that group's partition parallelism.
interview: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.

title: At-least-once vs at-most-once
short: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.
answer: Exactly-once must be considered end-to-end. Idempotent processing is often the practical target.
interview: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.

title: Service mesh
short: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.
answer: It can provide mTLS, routing and telemetry but adds platform complexity.
interview: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.

title: Debug production 500
short: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.
answer: Check trace ID, stack trace, deployment/config changes, downstream and DB errors before restarting.
interview: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.

title: Prevent cascading failures
short: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.
answer: Unlimited waiting exhausts threads/connections; isolation prevents blast radius.
interview: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.

title: Blue-green deployment
short: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.
answer: Rollback is fast, but database migrations must remain compatible during transition.
interview: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.

title: Canary deployment
short: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.
answer: Use health and business metrics as rollout gates.
interview: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.

title: Distributed lock
short: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.
answer: Leases/expiration and failure semantics are essential. Idempotency may be safer than locking.
interview: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.

title: Strangler pattern
short: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.
answer: Route capabilities to new components, validate, then retire legacy paths.
followups: When is it better than rewrite?
interview: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.

title: Persistence context
short: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.
answer: It provides identity semantics and dirty checking for managed entities.
interview: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.

title: Entity states
short: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
answer: Lifecycle state explains persist, merge, detach and remove behavior.
interview: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.

title: persist vs merge
short: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.
answer: merge does not simply reattach the same object.
interview: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.

title: Lazy vs eager fetching
short: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.
answer: Lazy can cause N+1/LazyInitializationException; eager can over-fetch.
interview: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.

title: N+1 query problem
short: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.
answer: Fix with fetch joins, EntityGraphs, batch fetching or projections.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer
interview: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.

title: @Version optimistic locking
short: A version field detects concurrent updates.
answer: Hibernate includes the version in update conditions and increments it.
interview: A version field detects concurrent updates.

title: JPQL
short: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.
answer: Use native SQL when database-specific features or specialized queries are justified.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.status=:status
interview: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.

title: EntityGraph
short: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.
answer: It avoids making relationships globally eager.
interview: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.

title: Dirty checking
short: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.
answer: Within a transaction, changing a managed entity can be enough.
interview: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.

title: Spring Data JPA save()
short: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.
answer: New-state detection depends on entity metadata/state. SQL may be deferred.
interview: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.

title: flush vs commit
short: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.
answer: A flush can send SQL while the transaction can still roll back.
followups: Why can a constraint fail at flush?
interview: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.

title: Cascade types
short: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.
answer: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH and ALL are available. This differs from DB FK cascades.
interview: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.

title: orphanRemoval
short: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.
answer: Use for composition-style ownership, not independent child lifecycles.
interview: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.

title: Optimize JPA-heavy endpoint
short: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.
answer: Treat generated SQL as a first-class performance artifact.
code: SELECT new com.example.OrderSummary(o.id,o.status) FROM Order o
interview: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.

title: LazyInitializationException
short: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.
answer: Use explicit fetch plans and DTO mapping inside a clear transaction boundary.
interview: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.

title: JWT structure
short: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.
answer: Header has metadata, payload has claims, signature protects integrity/authenticity. Base64URL is not encryption.
interview: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.

title: Authentication vs authorization
short: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.
answer: Roles, scopes and policies are authorization mechanisms.
interview: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.

title: CSRF
short: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.
answer: It is especially relevant to cookie-based authentication. CORS is not a general CSRF defense.
interview: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.

title: Password storage
short: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.
answer: bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 are typical choices. Never store plaintext or reversibly encrypted passwords.
interview: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.

title: OAuth 2.0
short: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.
answer: Authorization Code with PKCE is common for user-facing apps. OpenID Connect adds identity.
code: Client -> Authorization Server -> Token -> Resource Server
interview: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.

title: CORS
short: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.
answer: It is browser-enforced; server-side authorization is still required.
interview: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.

title: Refresh token
short: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.
answer: Refresh tokens need stronger protection, rotation and revocation strategies.
interview: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.

title: RBAC
short: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.
answer: Roles map identities to authorities. Complex systems may need policies/permissions.
interview: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.

title: Service-to-service security
short: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.
answer: mTLS, OAuth2 client credentials or workload identity are common approaches.
interview: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.

title: REST API security checklist
short: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.
answer: Review broken access control, injection, token handling, request limits and dependency vulnerabilities.
interview: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.

title: Reverse a string
short: Use StringBuilder.reverse() or a character loop.
answer: The straightforward approach is O(n).
interview: Use StringBuilder.reverse() or a character loop.

title: Palindrome check
short: Compare characters from both ends toward the center.
answer: Two pointers give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
interview: Compare characters from both ends toward the center.

title: First non-repeated character with Streams
short: Count characters while preserving encounter order, then select count 1.
answer: LinkedHashMap is important for first-occurrence order.
interview: Count characters while preserving encounter order, then select count 1.

title: Find duplicates using Streams
short: Use groupingBy/counting or a seen set.
answer: A seen set can detect repeats in encounter order; groupingBy is declarative.
interview: Use groupingBy/counting or a seen set.

title: Maximum salary by department
short: Group by department and select max salary.
answer: groupingBy plus maxBy directly models the requirement.
interview: Group by department and select max salary.

title: Group employees by department
short: Use Collectors.groupingBy.
answer: The result maps department to employee lists.
interview: Use Collectors.groupingBy.

title: Second highest distinct salary
short: Map salaries, distinct, sort descending, skip one.
answer: Distinct is required if 'second' means second distinct value.
interview: Map salaries, distinct, sort descending, skip one.

title: Longest name in each department
short: Group by department and choose max by name length.
answer: Use groupingBy plus maxBy.
interview: Group by department and choose max by name length.

title: Anagram check
short: Compare normalized character frequency maps or sorted characters.
answer: Frequency counting is expected O(n). Define normalization assumptions.
interview: Compare normalized character frequency maps or sorted characters.

title: Missing number 1..n
short: Use a long sum or XOR.
answer: The sum formula is simple; use long to avoid integer overflow under larger constraints.
interview: Use a long sum or XOR.

title: Word frequency with Streams
short: Normalize and group words with counting.
answer: Define case/punctuation rules before coding.
interview: Normalize and group words with counting.

title: Merge two sorted arrays
short: Use two pointers and take the smaller current value.
answer: This is O(n+m) for new output.
interview: Use two pointers and take the smaller current value.

title: Remove duplicates from sorted array
short: Use a slow write pointer.
answer: Sorted input enables O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
code: int w=1; for(int r=1;r<a.length;r++) if(a[r]!=a[r-1]) a[w++]=a[r];
interview: Use a slow write pointer.

title: First duplicate element
short: Track seen values and return the first repeated value.
answer: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space; clarify what first means.
code:
Set<Integer> seen=new HashSet<>();
for(int n:nums)if(!seen.add(n))return n;
interview: Track seen values and return the first repeated value.

title: Intersection of arrays
short: Use a set for membership or a frequency map when duplicates matter.
answer: For sorted arrays, two pointers are another O(n+m) option.
interview: Use a set for membership or a frequency map when duplicates matter.

title: LRU cache concept
short: Combine O(1) hash lookup with recency ordering.
answer: HashMap plus doubly linked list is classic; LinkedHashMap can implement access-order behavior.
interview: Combine O(1) hash lookup with recency ordering.

title: Top K frequent elements
short: Count frequencies and maintain a min-heap of size K.
answer: This gives O(n log k) after counting.
interview: Count frequencies and maintain a min-heap of size K.

title: Linked-list cycle detection
short: Use Floyd slow/fast pointers.
answer: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
interview: Use Floyd slow/fast pointers.

title: Binary search
short: Repeatedly halve a sorted search interval.
answer: Keep boundary conventions consistent and use overflow-safe midpoint calculation.
interview: Repeatedly halve a sorted search interval.

title: Balanced parentheses
short: Use a stack to match each closing delimiter with the latest opening delimiter.
answer: The LIFO structure matches nesting naturally.
interview: Use a stack to match each closing delimiter with the latest opening delimiter.

title: How to start system design
short: Clarify requirements, scale, consistency, latency, availability and constraints.
answer: Restate functional requirements, estimate traffic/data, propose high-level architecture and drill into bottlenecks.
interview: Clarify requirements, scale, consistency, latency, availability and constraints.

title: Design a URL shortener
short: Store a unique short key to URL mapping and optimize reads with cache.
answer: Write persists mapping; reads check cache then DB. Discuss collisions, expiry and analytics.
interview: Store a unique short key to URL mapping and optimize reads with cache.

title: Design a rate limiter
short: Define allowance per identity using token bucket/sliding-window logic.
answer: For multiple instances, shared low-latency state or gateway enforcement may be needed.
interview: Define allowance per identity using token bucket/sliding-window logic.

title: Design notification service
short: Accept requests durably, queue work, deliver via provider adapters and track status.
answer: API + outbox + broker + workers + provider adapters; add retries/idempotency/DLQ.
interview: Accept requests durably, queue work, deliver via provider adapters and track status.

title: Design order management
short: Make order state durable and coordinate payment/inventory/fulfillment with local transactions.
answer: Order service owns state; outbox publishes events; Saga/state machine coordinates outcomes.
interview: Make order state durable and coordinate payment/inventory/fulfillment with local transactions.

title: Design file upload service
short: Use object storage, preferably direct signed uploads for large files.
answer: API creates signed URL; client uploads directly; async workers validate/process.
code: API -> signed URL -> Object Storage -> Worker
interview: Use object storage, preferably direct signed uploads for large files.

title: Caching design
short: Place caches at client/CDN/gateway/app/distributed layers based on need.
answer: Define key, TTL, invalidation, stampede protection and consistency.
interview: Place caches at client/CDN/gateway/app/distributed layers based on need.

title: High availability
short: Remove single points of failure with redundancy across critical components.
answer: Use multiple instances/zones, health checks and appropriate data replication.
interview: Remove single points of failure with redundancy across critical components.

title: CAP theorem practically
short: During a partition, you cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability for every operation.
answer: CAP describes partition behavior; different operations can make different trade-offs.
interview: During a partition, you cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability for every operation.

title: Database sharding
short: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.
answer: A good key distributes load and supports common access patterns; cross-shard queries add complexity.
interview: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.

title: Read replicas vs sharding
short: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.
answer: Replicas may lag; sharding complicates queries and rebalancing.
interview: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.

title: Eventual consistency in design
short: Reads can temporarily lag writes while replicas/events converge.
answer: Define acceptable stale windows and user-visible pending states.
interview: Reads can temporarily lag writes while replicas/events converge.

title: Capacity estimation
short: Translate users/actions into QPS, storage, bandwidth and peak requirements.
answer: State assumptions and use order-of-magnitude numbers.
interview: Translate users/actions into QPS, storage, bandwidth and peak requirements.

title: Backpressure
short: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers.
answer: Use bounded queues, flow control, batching, rate limits or load shedding.
interview: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers.

title: Observability by design
short: Design metrics, structured logs and trace context from day one.
answer: Include trace IDs, latency/error metrics, dependency timing and business counters.
interview: Design metrics, structured logs and trace context from day one.

title: Primary key
short: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.
answer: A table has one primary-key constraint, possibly composite.
code: CREATE TABLE student(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(100));
interview: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.

title: Primary vs unique key
short: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.
answer: Primary key columns are non-null. NULL semantics for unique constraints vary by DB.
code: ALTER TABLE student ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE(email);
interview: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.

title: Foreign key
short: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.
answer: It ensures references point to valid parent keys subject to null and action semantics.
interview: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.

title: Normalization
short: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.
answer: Normal forms improve integrity; intentional denormalization can help performance.
interview: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.

title: Indexes and write cost
short: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.
answer: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE may update several indexes. Use actual query plans to justify them.
interview: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.

title: Composite index
short: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.
answer: Design it around common predicates and sorting. It is not equivalent to separate single-column indexes.
interview: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.

title: WHERE vs HAVING
short: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.
answer: Use WHERE to reduce input and HAVING for aggregate conditions.
code: SELECT dept,AVG(salary) FROM employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary)>70000;
interview: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.

title: INNER vs LEFT JOIN
short: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.
answer: A WHERE predicate on the right table can turn a LEFT JOIN into an effective inner join.
code: SELECT c.id,o.id FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id;
interview: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.

title: Window functions
short: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.
answer: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, SUM OVER and LAG support analytics with row-level detail.
code: SELECT name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk FROM employee;
interview: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.

title: Find duplicate email/contact
short: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.
answer: SELECT email,contact_number,COUNT(*) cnt FROM student GROUP BY email,contact_number HAVING COUNT(*)>1;
interview: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.

title: Database transaction
short: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.
answer: Transactions protect atomicity and consistency while isolation controls concurrency.
code: BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
interview: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.

title: ACID
short: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.
answer: Atomicity is all-or-nothing; consistency preserves constraints; isolation controls concurrency; durability concerns committed data survival.
interview: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.

title: SQL deadlock
short: Transactions can wait cyclically for each other's locks.
answer: Databases may abort one transaction. Keep transactions short and use safe bounded retries.
code:
T1 locks A -> waits B
T2 locks B -> waits A

answer: Monitor heap usage trends over time — a genuine leak shows a steady climb that doesn't recover after GC.
